intro: Noor Haddad is a business analyst at Northwind Credit Union. After a phishing scare, the board asks every department to nominate someone to understand security, compliance and identity. Noor puts a hand up before anyone else can and then spends the weekend wondering what she volunteered for. SC-900 is the starting point.
Follow Noor through one very eventful quarter at Northwind, from the first phishing email to a clean audit.

security-compliance-concepts: The credit union is moving its HR app to the cloud. Noor’s first question: “So is security now the provider’s problem?” Not exactly. The provider looks after the building and the hardware; Northwind still decides who signs in and what data is stored. Noor learns that security is built in layers, that trust is never assumed, and that encryption and hashing are different things for different jobs.
identity-concepts: A supplier portal lets Northwind staff click “Sign in with your work account.” Noor watches as the work directory vouches for the employee and the supplier’s app trusts that vouching. Two questions are being answered in order: who are you, and what are you allowed to see? Noor learns the words for each, and why identity has become the new edge of the network.
entra-identities: Northwind’s staff accounts live in an on-premises directory, but everyone needs Microsoft 365. Noor learns how accounts are synchronised so each person has one identity, and how apps can get their own identities without passwords. She also learns the difference between employees, guests from partner organisations, and the machine identities no one thinks about until something breaks.
entra-authentication: After the phishing scare, the board wants everyone to use something stronger than a password. Noor learns about the second factor, the authenticator app, passkeys, and sign-in methods without passwords at all. For the small satellite branch with basic licences, there is a simple default that switches protection on for everyone. For the main office, there is a more flexible approach with banned passwords and self-service reset.
entra-access-governance: Finance staff must use extra verification from outside the office. Noor learns the safe way to roll that out: start with a policy that only reports what it would have done, check the logs, then enforce. She also meets the idea of administrators who are only eligible for powerful roles and activate them for a short time, and of regular reviews to remove access nobody needs any more.
azure-infrastructure-security: The new customer portal goes into Azure. Noor sketches its protection like a castle: a filter at the front door for web attacks, protection against floods of traffic, rules separating the web and database areas, a controlled way for administrators to log in without exposing anything, and a safe for keys and secrets. Each defence has one job, and none is expected to do them all.
defender-for-cloud: Northwind’s workloads sit in more than one cloud. Noor connects them to a single dashboard that gives a score for how well the environment is configured, and a ranked list of the fixes that would raise it most. She also sees how it maps routes an attacker might take, and how it can keep remote desktop ports closed until someone needs them.
microsoft-sentinel: Logs from sign-ins, email, firewalls and the cloud all land in one place. Noor sees a rule that spots someone signing in from two countries within an hour, raises an incident, and automatically disables the account while alerting the security team. Analysts can also go hunting through the data for things no rule has caught yet. She learns the two acronyms that describe this: one for collecting and analysing, one for responding automatically.
defender-xdr: A staff member clicks a phishing link. The link is blocked at the moment of the click, but another route has already put malware on a laptop. Noor watches as separate protections for email, devices, identities and cloud apps each notice a piece of the story, and a single portal stitches them into one incident. She learns why “extended” detection is about connecting signals.
service-trust-privacy: Audit season. The auditor wants evidence about the cloud provider’s own security certifications and how Northwind meets a regulation. Noor learns where the provider publishes its audit reports, how privacy principles guide what is done with customer data, and how a compliance score shows which actions would close the gaps. She assigns the actions to teams and watches the score climb.
information-protection: The legal team wants a “Client Confidential” label that encrypts documents and travels with them. Noor learns how data can be found and classified, how labels are published, how rules can stop labelled files being emailed outside, and how retention rules keep or delete things on a schedule. Everything is aimed at one question: what does Northwind own, and how should it be treated?
insider-ediscovery-audit: An engineer who has handed in notice is copying files to a personal cloud account. Noor sees how an insider risk alert becomes a case. Later, a lawsuit arrives: she learns how legal can search across mailboxes and files, place holds so nothing is deleted, and export what is needed, with an audit trail of who did what and when.

epilogue: The audit comes back clean. Noor has gone from “what is a tenant?” to explaining Zero Trust to the board in plain words. On exam day she is nervous, but then she reads the first question and realises it is about a problem she has already seen, with different names on it.
